case_name: Sir Mortimer B. Davis Jewish General Hospital c. A.T.
text:
Sir Mortimer B. Davis Jewish
General Hospital c. A.T.

2020 QCCS 2149

JB4784

SUPERIOR COURT

CANADA

PROVINCE OF QUEBEC

DISTRICT OF

MONTREAL

No:

500-17-112233-203

DATE:

10 July 2020

______________________________________________________________________

IN THE PRESENCE OF:

THE HONOURABLE

BABAK BARIN, J.S.C.

______________________________________________________________________

SIR MORTIMER B. DAVIS JEWISH GENERAL
HOSPITAL

and

DR. LOUISE MINER

Plaintiffs

v.

A. T.

Defendant

and

H. G.

Interested Person (Husband)

____________________________________________________________________

PSYCHIATRIC EVALUATION
ORDER

Articles 10, 11 and 16
C.C.Q.

______________________________________________________________________

INTRODUCTION

[
1
]

At law, self-determination of a person of age generally
prevails over effective medical treatment. No matter how ill that person, how
likely possible the deterioration of their condition or even possible death, it
is usually only for that person to decide whether or not to accept a proposed
medical treatment. Where the person lacks the capacity to make the decision, however,
the law steps in to address the situation. There is no one fits all or an easy answer
to the question of when a person is incapable of making a decision relating to their
treatment or when precisely the law should step in to overtake it.
[1]
Varying situations have necessitated varying
answers.

[
2
]

In Quebec, articles 10 ,11 and 16 C.C.Q. legislate similar
notions:

10.

Principle
.
Every person is inviolable and is entitled to the integrity of his person.

Invasion
.
Except in cases provided for by law, no
one may interfere with his person without his free and enlightened consent
.

11.

Consent
to care
.
No one may be made to undergo care of any nature, whether
for examination
, specimen taking, removal of tissue,
treatment or other
act, except with his consent
. Except as otherwise provided by law, the
consent is subject to no other formal requirement and may be withdrawn at any
time, even verbally.

[…]

16.
Authorization of court
.

The authorization of the court is
necessary where the person
who may give consent to care required by the state of health of a minor person
or a person of full age who is incapable of giving his consent is prevented
from doing so or, without justification refuses to do so; it is also
necessary
where a person of full age who is incapable of giving his consent categorically
refuses to receive care
, except in the case of hygienic care and emergency.

[…]

[Underlining is mine]

[
3
]

There is no doubt that a psychiatric evaluation can
be qualified as an “examination”, a “treatment” or “other act” of a medical
nature as encapsulated in article 11 C.C.Q., and that such evaluation requires
the prior consent of the person who is to be evaluated. There is equally no
doubt that the court can substitute the consent of that person, if he or she is
incapable of providing it
and
categorically refuses to accept the
evaluation in question.

[
4
]

The issue in this case is whether the defendant,
Ms. A. T., 52 years old, lacks the capacity to consent to undergo the psychiatric
evaluation requested by the Sir Mortimer B. Davis Jewish General Hospital.
Pursuant to two sequential confinement orders obtained during the month of February
2020, Ms. A. T. spent thirty (30) days at the Jewish General Hospital. While at
the hospital, she categorically refused to undergo a psychiatric evaluation.
She continues to do so today.

BACKGROUND

[
5
]

On 12 February 2020, following a minor car collision
near the intersection of Chemin Queen Mary and Chemin Circle at around 7:30
p.m., considering the mental condition in which she found herself after the
fender bender, the police considered it necessary to take Ms. A. T. to the Jewish
General Hospital. According to the accident report filed, Ms. A. T. showed symptoms
of paranoia and complained of being followed by hearses and, in particular, a
Mercedes Benz that had been pursuing her since Westmount for the past 14 years.

[
6
]

On 17 February 2020, considering that Ms. A. T.
refused to undergo the psychiatric evaluation recommended by Dr. Marsha Heyman,
the Honourable Yves Hamel J.C.Q. issued a temporary confinement order directing
Ms. A. T. to undergo such evaluation. Ten days later, based on the reports of
Dr. Karl Looper and Dr. Rachel Kronick and considering that Ms. A. T. refused to
remain at the hospital, the confinement order was renewed by the Honourable Brigitte
Gouin J.C.Q. for 30 days.

[
7
]

Dr. Looper’s 17 February 2020 report reads in relevant
parts as follows:

History from the chart including
reports from the family and police. 52 year woman with no previous contact with
psychiatry, but having many years of paranoia

including believing that she is followed, listened to, watched. Mostly isolated
herself to home. Brought to the hospital by police and urgence psychosociale
after a minor car accident that led to an altercation with the other driver
when she became paranoid of him. She allegedly drove her car towards him twice
in a threatening way and inappropriately approached his young daughter who was
sitting in the car.

Pressured and rapid speech, no
insight,
does not acknowledge any mental health issues. Uncooperative with
the interview, refusing to answer questions, demands to end the interview
.

Diagnosis:        Psychotic disorder

Severe [mental disorder] with
persisting paranoia, behaviour influenced by psychosis, no insight.

[Underlining is mine]

[
8
]

Dr. Kronick’s report a day later concludes:

52 year old woman with
over a
decade of long history of paranoid delusions
; believes that she is being persecuted
by a certain family and is being watched, filmed, listened to. Has pursued
multiple investigations. Has isolated herself at home – only leaves to get
groceries if someone is guarding house. […]

Speaks quickly, tangential and
over-inclusive in thought-form. Firmly believes she is “harassed” by the “main
perpetrator” who has been stalking her home and family […] for many years.
Denies being agitated or in any way aggressive after the MVA.
No insight and
poor judgment
.

Diagnosis:        Psychotic disorder

[Underlining is added]

[
9
]

On 1 March 2020, Ms. A. T. filed an appeal of Gouin J.’s decision before the Court of Appeal seeking, in
particular, the revision of the confinement portion of the order. That appeal
is still pending. In the meantime, on 13 March 2020, Ms. A. T. was released
from the hospital against medical advice. She posed, however, no immediate
risk.

[
10
]

While at the Jewish General Hospital, Ms. A. T.
was placed under the direct care of Dr. Paul Chan, a psychiatrist with more
than 40 years of experience. Dr. Chan who was able to spend several hours with
Ms. A. T. over the course of her stay at the hospital, inscribed the following
remarks in Ms. A. T.’s release notes from the hospital:

Patient had minor car accident and
involved with dispute with other driver. Some physical interaction. Long
history of paranoia.

Argumentative, uncooperative,
focused narrowly that she has a ‘record’ in hospital. Does not recognize she is
paranoid. No aggression. No threats.

Paranoid psychosis.

Persistent psychosis but no
immediate risk.

[
11
]

Following her discharge, on 26 March 2020, Ms. A.
T.’s lawyer sent a formal demand letter to the Jewish General Hospital
complaining about Dr. Chan and his conduct, and asked him to immediately cease harassment
and intimidation of his client. In that letter, Ms. A. T. also raised a concern
about Dr. Chan meeting with her two daughters on 20 March 2020 without her or
her husband’s consent.

CONTEXT

[
12
]

Under the circumstances, and considering that
there was no longer an alliance between the patient and her physician, on 25 May
2020, the Jewish General Hospital filed an application before the Superior
Court, presentable on 4 June 2020, seeking to have Ms. A. T. psychiatrically
evaluated by another psychiatrist.

[
13
]

Dr. Chan’s report dated 14 May 2020 filed in
support of that application, offers useful insight about the mental state of Ms.
A. T. collected through anecdotes recounted by her husband and two daughters. The
relevant excerpts read as follows:

Introduction/social context
of the patient

Ms. A. T. is a married woman living
with her husband, and her younger daughter, Ms. M. G. She has another daughter
named T. G. She is a housewife although was educated and [has] training as an
engineer. The author of this report has no other information because
Ms. A.
T. has refused formal interviews
.

Diagnosis

Ms. A. T. suffers from a
psychiatric diagnosis of paranoia.

Medical history

There is no relevant medical or
psychiatric history.

History of the
hospitalization of February 12 until March 13 2020

Ms. A. T. was brought to hospital
on February 12, 2020 by the police […] was put on antipsychotic Olanzapine 10
mg during her hospitalization but […] refused to take her medication.

She was released from hospital on
March 13, 2020 having been judged no longer a danger to herself or others. The
garde
en établissement
was lifted but we advised Ms. A. T. to remain at the
hospital. She was discharged against medical advice.

There is limited alliance with the
author of the report.

Ms. A. T. did not accept
treatment throughout the hospital stay
. Indeed she
believed she was kept in hospital inappropriately and while she accepted
discussions sometimes at length, usually in the hospital corridors or sometimes
in her room for a bit more privacy or to have less disruption,
she never
accepted to be formally interviewed such as sitting down face to face
.

We have met instead with her
husband and one of her daughters on several occasions and have had
communication through electronic means (email or texting), with knowledge and
permission from Ms. A. T.

[…]

Based on the information
obtained by husband and daughters, we understand Ms. A. T. has had psychiatric
symptoms primarily of a paranoid nature since 14 years
. There are innumerable instances of paranoid behaviour reported by
the husband but mostly by the 2 daughters, […] among the most significant are
enumerated below:

-

She believes the food is poisoned and will only
eat food that she makes from a limited diet, and drinks from water she has
boiled on the stove.

-

She watches surveillance cameras that have been
installed around the house and when the children were young, she would insist
for them to watch the cameras and they were told to stay in specific rooms of
the house with instructions to watch the outside windows.

[…]

-

She does not flush toilet paper from the
bathroom but keeps it in a bag and over the past 6 months has not flushed the
toilet.

[…]

-

There is no washing machine, dishwasher, fridge,
freezer in the house because she cannot allow repairmen into the house. The
family uses a mini fridge, toaster oven, and the children have slept in unclean
sheets for many years.

-

The mother keeps a knife at home to protect
herself and kept guns and a guard dog for protection. The house windows are
bulletproof.

[…]

-

The children have not had visitors to the house
for 8 years.

[…]

-

In the hospital, she was consumed by the fact
that she was kept in the hospital because of the accident. She can only focus
on the accident that brought her to hospital despite explanations that […] the
accident was less important than her subsequent behaviours.

[…]

-

She refused to be weighed because she would have
revealed personal information. She spoke of feeling punished by a “gang of
eight”. She was suspicious of the motives of the police and expressed distrust.
She spoke of the “system” being against her, and the hospital behaviour raising
“red flags”.

Required
treatment

-

A psychiatric evaluation is necessary to have
the opportunity to obtain a formal interview with Ms. A. T. to obtain all
required information and if need be, to ensure that she receives the required
treatment plan;

-

The designated psychiatrist must be able to
speak to Ms. A. T.’s daughters and Mr. A. T. to complete the psychiatric
evaluation;

-

The information obtained during the recent
hospitalization and presented in this report is worrisome and indicates that
there is probably a need for treatment;

[…]

-

We asked Ms. A. T. to meet with another
psychiatrist at the Jewish General Hospital due to the absence of a therapeutic
alliance between Ms. A. T. and the author of the report.

[…]

Incapacity
to consent to the treatment plan (a psychiatric evaluation)

During
her hospitalization, Ms. A. T. has demonstrated that she has no appreciation
that her beliefs and significant aspects of all her behaviour is the result of her
probable illness. Her judgment is severely impaired by her symptoms.
She is
thus unable to appreciate the purpose of a psychiatric evaluation as well as
the risks and benefits of it […] and is unable to appreciate that she is sick
.

Categorical
Refusal

There
is categorical refusal to undergo a psychiatric evaluation
.

Conclusion

Ms. A.
T. has an illness that […] appears to have a negative impact upon her daily
functioning and has impaired her ability to function adequately according to her
level of ability and it is clear that she can become a danger to herself and
others. She left the hospital against clinical advice on March 13, 2020.
It
is important that Ms. A. T. undergo a psychiatric evaluation despite her
categorical refusal
in order to confirm, with the necessary information at
hand, the need for a treatment plan and if required, seek a court order to
provide the treatment plan. Given the lack of trust towards the author of this
report and from Ms. A. T.’s husband, it is appropriate to involve another
psychiatrist at the Jewish General Hospital.

[Underlining
is added, underlining of the bold title text is of the original text]

[
14
]

On 4 June 2020, as scheduled, the lawyer for the
Jewish General Hospital and Dr. Chan appeared before me for the first time. Neither
Ms. A. T. nor her husband, Mr. H. G., were present, even though proof of
service of the proceedings filed indicated that they were properly notified.

[
15
]

At the hearing, Dr. Chan who was declared an
expert testified, among other things, that in his opinion, Ms. A. T. suffered
from paranoia and she did not have the capacity to understand and appreciate
the need and utility of a psychiatric evaluation.

[
16
]

After hearing the testimony of Dr. Chan and
considering the importance of the issue, the lawyer for the Jewish General
Hospital, who had previously offered to reach Mr. H. G. by telephone in the
court room, was asked to call him. An attempt to reach Ms. A. T. directly at
the telephone number offered by her husband was unsuccessful.

[
17
]

During the call with Mr. H. G., he was advised
that the hearing of the Jewish General Hospital’s application for a psychiatric
evaluation of his wife was going to be rescheduled to 23 June 2020 so as to
allow him and his wife to appear before the court. At the same time, Mr. H. G.
was also told that it was imperative for both he and his wife to be present at the
hearing so that they may offer their views about the request filed by the
hospital.  A similar message was transmitted to Ms. A. T. and Mr. H. G. through
Mr. H. G.’s lawyer during the case management conference call that took place on
22 June 2020.

[
18
]

Despite the above, neither Ms. A. T. nor anyone
on her behalf appeared at the 23 June 2020 hearing. Mr. H. G. and his personal lawyer,
however, came to court. Dr. Chan was also available at the hospital by
videoconference.

[
19
]

At the hearing, Mr. H. G. testified, among other
things, that although he was not opposed to his wife undergoing a psychiatric evaluation
– “there would likely be a benefit in having one done” – he was opposed to any
form of medication being administered to her.

[
20
]

Mr. H. G. described his spouse of 23 years as
highly intelligent and capable of doing almost anything. He also described her
as having “a few issues” but then added: “who doesn’t?”

[
21
]

Mr. H. G. also testified that Ms. A. T. had
categorically refused to submit herself to a psychiatric evaluation, which he
did not find urgently needed under the current health conditions in any event,
and added that “he hoped that she would one day agree to it on her own
volition”.

[
22
]

Mr. H. G. concluded by saying that there was not
much more he could do for his wife under the circumstances.

ANALYSIS

[
23
]

As indicated earlier, it is trite that a psychiatric evaluation is an examination, treatment or other act of a
medical nature as provided for in the C.C.Q. The only
issue that requires determination in this case is whether Ms. A. T. lacks the capacity
to consent to the psychiatric evaluation
and
whether she categorically
refuses to undergo that evaluation. If so, the court can intervene, otherwise
the hospital’s request must be denied.
[2]

[
24
]

To begin with, two brief preliminary remarks are
in order. First, there is no presumption in law to the effect that a person who
is undergoing psychiatric treatment is inapt to consent to the care that may be
required by that person’s state of health.
[3]

[
25
]

The fact that a person is mentally ill does not
always prevent him or her from being able to consent to certain types of
treatment. That person may be able to consent to a particular treatment at one
time but not another. The person’s ability to consent may be present under
certain circumstances but not others.
[4]

It is also possible that that person may be capable of consenting to treatment
when on medication, but not when medication is discontinued.
[5]
Every case turns on its own
facts.

[
26
]

Second, the right for an individual to decide
their own medical fate entitles that person to direct the course of their own
care: It is this principle that underlies the concept of informed consent and
is protected by
section 7
of the
Canadian
Charter of Rights and Freedoms
.
[6]
The
right to medical self-determination is not vitiated by the fact that serious
risks or consequences, including death, may flow from an individual’s decision.

Section 7
, “does not promise that the state will never interfere with a
person’s life, liberty or security […] – laws do that all the time – but rather
that the state will not do so in a way that violates the principle of
fundamental justice.”
[7]

[
27
]

To reiterate again, the intervention of the
court in matters such as this depends on the satisfaction of two factors – lack
of capacity to give consent and categorical refusal.
[8]
If one or the other is
missing, the court cannot intervene.
[9]

[
28
]

The issue of capacity to give consent is a
question of fact that must be examined in light of, among others perhaps, the
following five questions. Does the individual understand the nature of the
illness for which treatment is being proposed? Does he or she understand the
nature and goal of the treatment? Does the person appreciate the risks and
advantages of the treatment offered? What about the consequences of not
following the treatment? Is the individual’s lack of capacity to consent in any
way affected by his or her illness?
[10]

[
29
]

In a way, the above questions summarize the two
aspects of capacity described as follows. First, the person “must be able to
understand the information that is relevant to making a treatment decision.
This requires the cognitive ability to process, retain and understand the relevant
information.”
[11]

Second, the person “must be able to appreciate the reasonably foreseeable
consequences of the decision or lack of one. This requires the [person] to be
able to apply the relevant information to his or her circumstances and be able
to weigh the foreseeable risks and benefits of a decision or lack thereof.”
[12]

[
30
]

Once there is a finding of incapacity, it is
only in the face of categorical refusal that the court can intervene. The
treatment in question must have been specifically offered and not simply
envisaged.

[
31
]

Whether or not the matter is contested, and
whether or not the person is present, such as in this case, the court must
conduct a scrupulous investigation, bearing in mind the guidance offered in
article 12 C.C.Q. and not taking on the role or place of the treating physician
or physicians.

[
32
]

The role of the court is not to find or propose
an appropriate or alternative treatment but to ensure that that which is being offered
corresponds to the directions found in article 12.
[13]

12.

Consent
for other
.
A person who gives his consent to or refuses care for
another person is bound to act in the sole interest of that person, taking into
account, as far as possible, and wishes the latter may have expressed.

Consent for other.
If he gives his consent, he shall ensure that the care is
beneficial notwithstanding the gravity and the permanence of certain of its
effects, that is advisable in the circumstances and that the risks incurred are
not disproportionate to the anticipated benefits.

[
33
]

Moreover, it is not for the court to set aside
an already completed medical evaluation or assessment unless there is
justification to do so
[14]
.
In situations where the person for whom treatment is being sought is
unavailable or absent, the work of the court becomes more onerous. Alternative
submissions concerning the evidence filed and the law applicable will not be available.
In any event, the overall exercise is not an easy one, and it requires rigour,
courage and empathy.

[
34
]

As in any case, the onus of proof on the balance
of probabilities at the so-called capacity evaluation hearing, is on the person
seeking to obtain the evaluation or asking to impose the treatment in question.
Like in any case, the court may also, in its discretion, draw positive or
negative inferences as the facts of the case may warrant. It is important to recall
that psychiatry is not an exact science and that the care requested must appear
to be beneficial for the person intended.

Categorical
refusal

[
35
]

While this is the second part of a two-prong test
under article 16 C.C.Q., I will deal with it first because it is clear and
there is not much to be said about it.

[
36
]

In this case, there is no doubt that Ms. A. T.
has categorically refused to undergo the psychiatric evaluation recommended by
Dr. Chan, who had the benefit of spending time with her and observing her. The
reports of Dr. Looper and Dr. Chan highlight this point. There is also no doubt
that Ms. A. T. categorically refuses to undergo a psychiatric evaluation today.

[
37
]

The absence of Ms. A. T. before the court on two
separate occasions, despite the court’s specific request – but
not
order
– that she be present at the 23 June 2020 hearing is demonstrative of this
point. It is implicitly clear that Ms. A. T. does not approve of the hospital’s
initiative and the psychiatric evaluation requested and that she is refusing it.

[
38
]

There is therefore no doubt that one of the two
elements required by article 16 C.C.Q. is satisfied on the balance of
probabilities.

Lack of
capacity to consent

[
39
]

The thorny question that remains is whether Ms. A.
T. is capable of consenting to the psychiatric evaluation requested by the
Jewish General Hospital.

[
40
]

In his report of 14 May 2020, Dr. Chan, a psychiatrist
of some forty plus years of experience, and the only person in the context of
these proceedings – except for Mr. H. G. of course who shares a permanent roof
with Ms. A. T. – who has had the benefit of spending considerable time with Ms.
A. T., concludes that “she is unable to appreciate the purpose of a psychiatric
evaluation as well as [its] risks and benefits […] and she is unable to
appreciate that she is sick.”

[
41
]

As for Mr. H. G., while in the same breath he candidly
expresses the wish that Ms. A. T. herself reach the conclusion that a
psychiatric evaluation is needed, he also indicates that his wife is capable of
doing almost anything, even though she has issues like everyone else. This
nuanced answer unfortunately is not helpful to the court.

[
42
]

In the absence of any evidence put forth by Ms. A.
T. herself, and in the absence of the court’s ability to observe Ms. A. T.’s
behaviour in person, the probative value of Mr. H. G.’s statement is not enough
to displace the evidence that Dr. Chan and the other treating physicians of Ms.
A. T. have put forward in this case.

[
43
]

Had Ms. A. T. appeared in court on 23 June 2020,
as it was expected that she would in response to the explicit request of the
court, she would have perhaps been able to convince the court that she has the
capacity to consent to the psychiatric evaluation requested, and that it is
perhaps unwarranted under the present circumstances. Unfortunately, she did
not.

[
44
]

Consequently, the only reasonable conclusion that
the court can arrive at in light of the evidence offered is that Ms. A. T.
lacks the capacity to consent to the psychiatric evaluation requested by the
Jewish General Hospital. The result then is that the hospital’s application
must be granted.

[
45
]

The court is also of the view that the psychiatric
evaluation requested by the hospital is beneficial for Ms. A. T., it certainly
appears to be advisable in the circumstances and its benefits appear to significantly
outweigh any possible risks that may be associated with it.

Appointment
of a new psychiatrist

[
46
]

In light of the fact that there is a breakdown
in the therapeutic alliance between Dr. Chan and Ms. A. T., and furthermore,
that Dr. Chan has been formally put on notice by Ms. A. T.’s lawyer, the court
agrees with the Jewish General Hospital that another physician must be
appointed to conduct the psychiatric evaluation of Ms. A. T.

[
47
]

To that end, at the 23 June 2020 hearing, the
court was provided with a copy of Dr. Robert Simon Biskin’s extensive
curriculum vitae comprised of 18 pages.

[
48
]

This document indicates, among other things,
that Dr. Biskin is an experienced psychiatrist and an assistant professor in
the Department of Psychiatry of the Faculty of Medicine of McGill University.
Based on the information before the court and considering that there has been
no objection to the appointment of Dr. Biskin, the court appoints Dr. Biskin as
the psychiatrist to evaluate Ms. A. T. in this matter.

[
49
]

Moreover, considering that Mr. H. G. is an
interested party with whom Dr. Biskin may need to talk to as part of his
evaluation, a copy of all exhibits filed in this matter may be shared with him
and his lawyer.

[
50
]

Ms. A. T. must now attend at the Institute of
Community and Family Psychiatry (
ICFP
) of the Jewish General Hospital
located at 4333 Chemin de la Côte-Sainte-Catherine, Montreal, Quebec H3T 1E2,
Room
143
, on Tuesday, 21 July 2020 at 9:00 a.m. to be psychiatrically evaluated
by Dr. Biskin.

[
51
]

Ms. A. T. is reminded that she must cooperate
with Dr. Biskin so as to provide him with an adequate opportunity to carry out
his evaluation, which may require more than one appointment. Ms. A. T. must
also be reminded that the evaluation is in her best interest and offers, as
indicated earlier, benefits that appear to significantly outweigh any possible
risks associated with it.

[
52
]

In advance of the July 21 appointment, in
addition to the exhibits filed in this judgement, Dr. Biskin must also have access
to Ms. A. T.’s psychiatric medical file at the Jewish General Hospital and be
provided with a copy of this judgment. As part of the psychiatric evaluation,
and as requested by the hospital, Dr. Biskin is also permitted, at his
discretion, to interview Mr. H. G. and Ms. A. T.’s adult children. The authority
granted to Dr. Biskin, however, must under no circumstance be unreasonably used.

[
53
]

It is also imperative for Ms. A. T. to
understand that she must comply with the terms of this judgment and attend at
the appointment that is confirmed for her with Dr. Biskin on July 21. If she
does not present herself at that appointment, the hospital is permitted to use
the assistance of a competent peace officer to take Ms. A. T. to the ICFP on
Wednesday, 22 July 2020 at 4 p.m. The same applies to all other follow up
appointments that may be fixed for Ms. A. T. until her psychiatric evaluation
is completed.

[
54
]

Finally, considering the history and particular
circumstances of this matter, I am of the view that the provisional execution
of this judgment notwithstanding appeal is justified. These situations are
never easy. While there is no rush and no immediate risk of harm by or for Ms. A.
T., everyone in Ms. A. T.’s immediate family circle, and most important of all,
she herself, has an interest in the completion of the evaluation in question. As
Dr. Chan explicitly sets out in his 14 May 2020 report, the purpose of the
evaluation is to confirm, with the necessary information in hand, whether or
not a treatment plan is required for Ms. A. T., and if so, provide her with
such a plan.

FOR THESE
REASONS, THE COURT:

GRANTS
the Plaintiffs’ Originating Application to obtain authorization from
the court for treatment (a psychiatric evaluation) of the defendant, Ms. A. T.;

CONFIRMS
the defendant, Ms. A. T.’s lack of capacity to consent and her
categorical refusal to undergo a psychiatric evaluation;

ORDERS
the defendant, Ms. A. T., to undergo a psychiatric evaluation;

APPOINTS
Dr. Robert Simon Biskin, psychiatrist, as the physician who will
conduct the psychiatric evaluation of the defendant, Ms. A. T.;

AUTHORIZES
the communication of Ms. A. T.’s complete psychiatric medical file
at the Sir Mortimer B. Davis Jewish General Hospital to Dr. Robert Simon Biskin
for the purpose of the psychiatric evaluation;

AUTHORIZES
the Interested Party, Mr. H. G., to have access to the exhibits of
the Plaintiff’s Originating Application to obtain authorization from the court
for treatment (a psychiatric evaluation) of the defendant, Ms. A. T.;

AUTHORIZES
